vo_text: A robot built to last ninety days on Mars kept going for more than fourteen years.
Why did it survive so long, and what finally stopped it?
Mars does not crush machines. It does not melt them.
It wears them down slowly in ways you already know from home.
The cold that kills a phone battery, the dust on a windscreen,
a tire that finally splits.
So could a robot survive on Mars? Could Orbit?
In this film, I will show you what Mars does to the machines we send,
how some of them lasted far longer than anyone
planned, and what it really takes to stay alive there.
At first glance, Mars looks like a desert you could drive across. Red
rock, rolling dunes, a hazy sky. It is a trick of the eye.
The air is so thin that the pressure at the ground is less than one percent of Earth's.
The average temperature is about minus sixty degrees.
At the first Viking landing site, nights fell to nearly minus ninety.
And because the air is thin and Mars has no global magnetic
shield, radiation reaches the ground. Curiosity
measured it. In one day on Mars, the dose
is roughly what you would get in three months on Earth.
A person would need a pressure suit just to stand there.
But a robot does not breathe, and it does not get
sick. So the thin air and the radiation
are not what usually ends a robot's life on Mars.
The killers are quieter: cold,
dust, wear. Of the robots that landed
safely and went to work, most were stopped by one of those three.
And whatever goes wrong, nobody can rush to help. A radio signal
takes from about three minutes to more than twenty to cross between the planets
each way. Nobody can steer a rover live like a toy car.
Every robot on Mars has to look after itself between messages from home.
Start with the cold because you have felt what it does.
Take your phone out on a freezing day and watch the battery
drop. Electronics and batteries hate deep cold.
On Mars, every night is colder than any winter night in a British
garden, so a rover spends part of its power
just keeping its own insides warm, like a person burning energy to shiver.
That only works while power keeps coming in.
In 2009, the rover Spirit drove into soft sand
at a place the team called Troy, and its wheels sank. It could not climb
out. It could not tilt its solar panels towards the low winter sun.
As the days shortened, its power fell. On the
22nd of March, 2010, Spirit sent its last message.
Spirit did not break apart. It got stuck, and
winter did the rest. Its mission had been planned for
ninety days. It worked for more than six years.
The cold can be even more direct. In 2008,
the Phoenix lander touched down near the North Pole of Mars to dig for ice.
When winter came, it went silent. Two years later, a spacecraft in
orbit photographed it again. Its solar panels looked broken,
most likely bent by the weight of frost and ice that had built up over the winter.
We make one of these every week.
Subscribing is how the next one finds you.
Spirit had a twin on the far side of Mars. It lasted
much longer, and the reason was the wind.
Mars is a dusty world. Fine red dust settles on everything, including
solar panels. A panel under dust is like a windscreen nobody wipes.
Less and less light gets through. A rover that runs on sunlight slowly starves.
Opportunity should have starved within months. Instead, again and again, Martian
wind and passing dust devils swept its panels clean. The team
called them cleaning events. Each one gave the rover back its power, and it kept driving.
Ninety days became years. Years became more than fourteen.
Then, in 2018, a storm grew until it wrapped the whole planet.
The sky over Opportunity grew so dark that almost no
sunlight reached its panels. On the 10th of June, 2018, Opportunity sent its
last signal. Engineers on Earth sent more than a thousand commands
over the next eight months asking it to wake up. It never answered.
What finally stopped the most successful rover of its time was not cold
or rock. It was the sky turning off.
Why does dust matter so much? Because on Mars, there is no
rain to wash anything clean. The lander InSight spent four
years listening for Mars quakes and felt more than a thousand of them. But dust
kept building on its panels. In December 2022,
it went quiet the same way. Not broken, just out of light.
Even a robot that never runs out of power wears out. Curiosity
runs on a nuclear power source, a small supply of plutonium that gives off heat
day and night, dust or no dust. When the 2018 storm
darkened Opportunity's sky, Curiosity kept working in another part of the planet.
But its wheels had a different problem. They are thin aluminum
made light enough to fly to Mars. In 2013, the team noticed
holes. Sharp rocks were punching through like a tire on broken
glass. Since then, the drivers have planned routes around the sharpest
ground, and they photograph the wheels to watch the damage grow.
Why not just build the wheels tougher? Because every kilogram has to be
launched off Earth, carried for months, slowed from thousands of kilometers an
hour, and set down gently on another world. On Mars,
strength always has to be weighed against getting there at all.
And then there is the little helicopter. Ingenuity was built for up to five
test flights over 30 days in air 1% as thick as ours.
It flew 72 times over almost three years. In January
2024, after its last landing, images showed damage to its rotor
blades. It could not fly again. It is still standing on Mars.
So could a robot survive on Mars? Yes.
Not forever, and not alone. The robots that last are the ones with a
steady supply of power, heaters to fight the night, and a team on
Earth who drive carefully around every sharp rock. Sometimes they
also need luck in the shape of a gust of wind at the right moment.
That is what Mars teaches. Survival there is not
one heroic moment. It is a thousand small decisions
made from another planet every single day.
What would Orbit need? Power that does not depend on a clear sky,
a way to stay warm through the night, a shell tough enough for sharp ground,
and someone at home watching. What if the real story of every
Mars robot is not how it died, but how long people kept it going?
The bigger question sits in the tracks they leave. Every robot that stops on Mars
stays exactly where it stopped, and the dust slowly covers it.
